The angle which <math>OE</math> makes with <math>OA</math> is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(C+D)</math> and that which <math>DC</math> makes is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(\pi+C+D)</math>; the angle <math>COE</math> is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(C-D)</math>. The sum of the projections of <math>OD</math> and <math>DE</math> on <math>OA</math> is equal to that of <math>OE</math>, and the sum of the projections of <math>OC</math> and <math>CE</math> is equal to that of <math>OE</math>; hence the sum of the projections of <math>OC</math> and <math>OD</math> is twice that of <math>OE</math>, or <math>\cos C+\cos D=2\cos\tfrac{1}{2}(C+D)\cos\tfrac{1}{2}(C-D)</math>. The difference of the projections of <math>OD</math> and <math>OC</math> an <math>OA</math> is equal to twice that of <math>ED</math>, hence we have the formula <math>\cos D-\cos C</math>

From any general relation between the sides and angles of a triangle other relations may be deduced by various methods of transformation, of which we give two examples.

<math>\alpha</math>. In any general relation between the sines and cosines of the angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> of a triangle we may substitute <math>pA+qB+rC</math>, <math>rA+pB+qC</math>, <math>qA+rB+pC</math> for <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively, where <math>p</math>, <math>q</math>, <math>r</math> are any quantities such that <math>p+q+r+1</math> is a positive or negative multiple of 6, provided that we change the signs of all the sines. Suppose <math>p+q+r+1=6n</math>, then the sum of the three angles <math>2n\pi-(pA+qB+rC)</math>, <math>2n\pi-(rA+pB+qC)</math>, <math>2n\pi-(qA+rB+pC)</math> is <math>\pi</math>; and, since the given relation follows from the condition <math>A+B+C=\pi</math>, we may substitute for <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively any angles of which the sum is <math>\pi</math>; thus the transformation is admissible.

<math>\beta</math>. It may easily be shown that the sides and angles of the triangle formed by joining the feet of the perpendiculars from the angular points <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> on the opposite sides of the triangle <math>ABC</math> are respectively <math>a\cos A</math>, <math>b\cos B</math>, <math>c\cos C</math>, <math>\pi-2A</math>, <math>\pi-2B</math>, <math>\pi-2C</math>; we may therefore substitute these expressions for <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively in any general formula. By drawing the perpendiculars of this second triangle and joining their feet as before, we obtain a triangle of which the sides are <math>-a\cos A\cos 2A</math>, <math>-b\cos B\cos 2B</math>, <math>-c\cos C\cos 2C</math> and the angles are <math>4A-\pi</math>, <math>4B-\pi</math>, <math>4C-\pi</math>; we may therefore substitute these expressions for the sides and angles of the original triangle; for example, we obtain thus the formula
{{block center|<math>\cos 4A = \frac{a^2\cos^2 A\cos^2 2A-b^2\cos^2 B\cos^2 2B-c^2\cos^2 C\cos^2 2C}{2bc\cos B\cos C\cos 2B\cos 2C}</math>.}}
This transformation obviously admits of further extension.

'''''Solution of Triangles.'''''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|274|TRIGONOMETRY|}}</noinclude>on a straight line making an angle <math>+\tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math> with <math>OD</math>, and is therefore equal to <math>OF \sin B</math>; hence

{{block center|<math>OF \cos(A+B) = OE \cos A + EF \cos(\tfrac{1}{2}\pi + A)</math>}}

{{block center|<math>= OF (\cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B),</math>}}

{{block center|or <math>\cos(A+B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B.</math>}}

The angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math> are absolutely unrestricted in magnitude, and thus this formula is perfectly general. We may change the sign of <math>B</math>, thus

{{block center|<math>\cos(A-B) = \cos A \cos(-B) - \sin A \sin(-B),</math>}}

{{block center|or <math>\cos(A-B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B.</math>}}

If we projected the sides of the triangle <math>OEF</math> on a straight line making an angle <math>+\tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math> with <math>OA</math> we should obtain the formulae

{{block center|<math>\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B,</math>}}

which are really contained in the cosine formula, since we may put <math>\tfrac{1}{2}\pi - B</math> for <math>B</math>. The formulae

{{block center|<math>\tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}, \cot(A \pm B) = \frac{\cot A \cot B \mp 1}{\cot B \pm \cot A}</math>}}

are immediately deducible from the above formulae. The equations

{{block center|<math>\sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C+D) \cos \tfrac{1}{2}(C-D),</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\sin C - \sin D = 2 \sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C-D) \cos \tfrac{1}{2}(C+D),</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\cos D + \cos C = 2 \cos \tfrac{1}{2}(C+D) \cos \tfrac{1}{2}(C-D),</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\cos D - \cos C = 2 \sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C+D) \sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C-D),</math>}} by the method of projections. Take <math>OC</math>, <math>OD</math>, making angles <math>C</math>, <math>D</math>, with <math>OA</math>, r to <math>CD</math>. The angle which <math>OE</math> makes with <math>OA</math> is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(C+D)</math> and that which <math>DC</math> makes is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(\pi+C+D)</math>; the angle <math>COE</math> is <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(C-D)</math>. The sum of the projections of <math>OD</math> and <math>DE</math> on <math>OA</math> is equal to that of <math>OE</math>, and the sum of the projections of <math>OC</math> and <math>CE</math> is equal to that of <math>OE</math>; hence the sum of the projections of <math>OC</math> and <math>OD</math> is twice that of <math>OE</math>, or <math>\cos C+\cos D=2\cos\tfrac{1}{2}(C+D)\cos\tfrac{1}{2}(C-D)</math>. The difference of the projections of <math>OD</math> and <math>OC</math> an <math>OA</math> is equal to twice that of <math>ED</math>, hence we have the formula <math>\cos D-\cos C</math> =2 <math>\sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C+D) \sin \tfrac{1}{2}(C-D)</math>. The other two formulae will be obtained by projecting on a straight line inclined at an angle <math>+\tfrac{1}{2}\pi</math> to <math>OA</math>.

[[File:eb1911 v27 p0289 c1f1.png|center|131px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 4.}}

As another example of the use of projections, we will find the sum of the series <math>\cos \alpha+\cos (\alpha+\beta)+\cos (\alpha+2\beta)+ \dots +\cos (\alpha+\overline{n-1}\beta)</math>. '''''Sum of Series of Cosines in Arithmetical Progression.''''' Suppose an unclosed polygon each angle of which is <math>\pi-\beta</math> to be inscribed in a circle, and let <math>A</math>, <math>A_1</math>, <math>A_2</math>, <math>A_3</math>, …, <math>A_n</math> be <math>n+1</math> consecutive angular points; let <math>D</math> be the diameter of the circle; and suppose a straight line drawn making an angle <math>\alpha</math> with <math>AA_1</math>, then <math>\alpha+\beta</math>, <math>\alpha+2\beta</math>, … are the angles it makes with <math>A_1 A_2</math>, <math>A_2</math>, <math>A_3</math>, …; we have by projections

{{block center|<math>AA_n \cos (\alpha+\tfrac{1}{2}\overline{n-1}\beta)=AA_1 \{\cos \alpha+ \cos \overline{\alpha+\beta+}\dots+\cos \alpha+\overline{(n-1)}\beta\}</math>,}}
{{block center|also <math>AA_1=\text{D} \sin \tfrac{1}{2}\beta,\ AA_n=D \sin \tfrac{1}{2}n\beta</math>;}}
hence the sum of the series of cosines is
{{block center|<math>\cos (\alpha+\overline{\tfrac{1}{2}n-1}\,\beta) \sin \tfrac{1}{2}n\beta \operatorname{cosec} \tfrac{1}{2}\beta</math>.}}
By a double application of the addition formulae we may obtain the formulae '''''Formulae for Sine and Cosine of Sum of Angles.'''''
{{block center|<math>\sin (A_1+A_2+A_3)=\sin A_1 \cos A_2 \cos A_3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\cos A_1 \sin A_2 \cos A_3+\cos A_1 \cos A_2 \sin A_3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>-\sin A_1 \sin A_2 \sin A_3</math>;}}
{{block center|<math>\cos (A_1+A_2+A_3)=\cos A_1 \cos A_2 \cos A_3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>-\cos A_1 \sin A_2 \sin A_3-\sin A_1 \cos A_2 \sin A_3</math>}}
{{block center|<math>-\sin A_1 \sin A_2 \cos A_3</math>.}}
We can by induction extend these formulae to the case of <math>n</math> angles.
{{block center|Assume <math>\sin (A_1+A_2+ \dots +A_n)=S_1-S_3+S_5- \dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\cos (A_1+A_2+ \dots +A_n)=S_0-S_2+S_4- \dots</math>}}
where <math>S_r</math> denotes the sum of the products of the sines of <math>r</math> of the angles and the cosines of the remaining <math>n-r</math> angles; then we have {{block center|<math>\sin (A_1+A_2+ \dots +A_n+A_{n+1}) = \cos A_{n+1}(S_1-S_3+S_5- \dots)</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+\sin A_{n+1}(S_0-S_2+S_4- \dots).</math>}}
The right-hand side of this equation may be written
{{block center|<math>(S_1 \cos A_{n+1}+S_0 \sin A_{n+1})-(S_3 \cos A_{n+1}+S_2 \sin A_{n+1})+ \dots,</math>}}
{{block center|or <math>S'_1-S'_3+ \dots</math>}}
where <math>S'_r</math> denotes the quantity which corresponds for <math>n+1</math> angles to <math>S_r</math> for <math>n</math> angles; similarly we may proceed with the cosine formula. The theorems are true for <math>n=2</math> and <math>n=3</math>; thus they are true generally. The formulae

'''''Formulae for Multiple and Sub-Multiple Angles.'''''
{{block center|<math>\cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2 \cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2 \sin^2 A,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\sin 2A = 2 \sin A \cos A, \qquad \tan 2A = \frac{2 \tan A}{1-\tan^2 A},</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\sin 3A = 3 \sin A - 4 \sin^3 A, \quad \cos 3A = 4 \cos^3 A - 3 \cos A,</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\sin nA = n \cos^{n-1} A \sin A - \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!} \cos^{n-3} A \sin^3 A + \dots</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(-1)^r \frac{n(n-1) \dots (n-2r)}{(2r+1)!} \cos^{n-2r-1} A \sin^{2r+1} A, \cos nA = \cos^n A - \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} \cos^{n-2} A \sin^2 A + \dots</math>}}

{{block center|<math>+ (-)^r \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-2r+1)}{2r!} \cos^{n-2r} A \sin^{2r} A + \dots</math>}}

may all be deduced from the addition formulae by making the angles all equal. From the last two formulae we obtain by division

{{block center|<math>\tan nA = \frac{n \tan A - \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!} \tan^3 A + \dots + (-1)^r \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-2r)}{(2r+1)!} \tan^{2r+1} A + \dots}{1 - \frac{n(n-1)}{2!} \tan^2 A + \dots + (-1)^r \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-2r+1)}{2r!} \tan^{2r} A + \dots}</math>}}

In the particular case of <math>n=3</math> we have <math>\tan 3A = \frac{3 \tan A - \tan^3 A}{1 - 3 \tan^2 A}</math>.

The values of <math>\sin \tfrac{1}{2}A</math>, <math>\cos \tfrac{1}{2}A</math>, <math>\tan \tfrac{1}{2}A</math> are given in terms of <math>\cos A</math> by the formulae

{{block center|<math>\sin \tfrac{1}{2} A = (-1)^p \left(\frac{1-\cos A}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}},\ \cos \tfrac{1}{2}A = (-1)^q \left(\frac{1+\cos A}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}},</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\tan \tfrac{1}{2} A = (-1)^r \left(\frac{1-\cos A}{1+\cos A}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}},</math>}}

where <math>p</math> is the integral part of <math>A/2\pi</math>, <math>q</math> the integral part of <math>A/2\pi + \tfrac{1}{2}</math>, and <math>r</math> the integral part of <math>A/\pi</math>. Sin <math>\tfrac{1}{2}A</math>, <math>\cos \tfrac{1}{2}A</math> are given in terms of <math>\sin A</math> by the formulae

{{block center|<math>2 \sin \tfrac{1}{2}A = (-1)^{p'}(1+\sin A)^{\frac{1}{2}} + (-1)^{q'}(1-\sin A)^{\frac{1}{2}},</math>}}

{{block center|<math>2 \cos \tfrac{1}{2}A = (-1)^{p'}(1+\sin A)^{\frac{1}{2}} - (-1)^{q'}(1-\sin A)^{\frac{1}{2}},</math>}} where <math>p'</math> is the integral part of <math>A/2\pi+\tfrac{1}{4}</math> and <math>q'</math> the integral part of <math>A/2\pi-\tfrac{1}{4}</math>.

'''''Properties of Triangles.'''''

6. In any plane triangle <math>ABC</math> we will denote the lengths of the sides <math>BC</math>, <math>CA</math>, <math>AB</math> by <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math> respectively, and the angles <math>BAC</math>, <math>ABC</math>, <math>ACB</math> by <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively. The fact that the projections of <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> on a straight line perpendicular to the side <math>a</math> are equal to one another is expressed by the equation <math>b \sin C=c \sin B</math>; this equation and the one obtained by projecting <math>c</math> and <math>a</math> on a straight line perpendicular to <math>a</math> may be written <math>a/\sin A=b/\sin B=c/\sin C</math>. The equation <math>a=b \cos C+c \cos B</math> expresses the fact that the side <math>a</math> is equal to the sum of the projections of the sides <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> on itself; thus we obtain the equations
{{block center|<math>\left.\begin{array}{l} a=b \cos C+c \cos B \\ b=c \cos A+a \cos C \\ c=a \cos B+b \cos A \end{array}\right\}</math>.}}
If we multiply the first of these equations by <math>-a</math>, the second by <math>b</math>, and the third by <math>c</math>, and add the resulting equations, we obtain the formula <math>b^2+c^2-a^2=2bc \cos A</math> or <math>\cos A=(b^2+c^2-a^2)/2bc</math>, which gives the cosine of an angle in terms of the sides. From this expression for <math>\cos A</math> the formulae
{{block center|<math>\sin \tfrac{1}{2}A=\left\{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{bc}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}},\ \cos \tfrac{1}{2}A=\left\{\frac{s(s-a)}{bc}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>,}}
{{block center|<math>\tan \tfrac{1}{2}A=\left\{\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}},\ \sin A=\frac{2}{bc}\{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)\}^{\frac{1}{2}}</math>,}} where <math>s</math> denotes <math>\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b+c)</math>, can be deduced by means of the dimidiary formula.

From any general relation between the sides and angles of a triangle other relations may be deduced by various methods of transformation, of which we give two examples.

<math>\alpha</math>. In any general relation between the sines and cosines of the angles <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> of a triangle we may substitute <math>pA+qB+rC</math>, <math>rA+pB+qC</math>, <math>qA+rB+pC</math> for <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively, where <math>p</math>, <math>q</math>, <math>r</math> are any quantities such that <math>p+q+r+1</math> is a positive or negative multiple of 6, provided that we change the signs of all the sines. Suppose <math>p+q+r+1=6n</math>, then the sum of the three angles <math>2n\pi-(pA+qB+rC)</math>, <math>2n\pi-(rA+pB+qC)</math>, <math>2n\pi-(qA+rB+pC)</math> is <math>\pi</math>; and, since the given relation follows from the condition <math>A+B+C=\pi</math>, we may substitute for <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively any angles of which the sum is <math>\pi</math>; thus the transformation is admissible.

<math>\beta</math>. It may easily be shown that the sides and angles of the triangle formed by joining the feet of the perpendiculars from the angular points <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> on the opposite sides of the triangle <math>ABC</math> are respectively <math>a\cos A</math>, <math>b\cos B</math>, <math>c\cos C</math>, <math>\pi-2A</math>, <math>\pi-2B</math>, <math>\pi-2C</math>; we may therefore substitute these expressions for <math>a</math>, <math>b</math>, <math>c</math>, <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> respectively in any general formula. By drawing the perpendiculars of this second triangle and joining their feet as before, we obtain a triangle of which the sides are <math>-a\cos A\cos 2A</math>, <math>-b\cos B\cos 2B</math>, <math>-c\cos C\cos 2C</math> and the angles are <math>4A-\pi</math>, <math>4B-\pi</math>, <math>4C-\pi</math>; we may therefore substitute these expressions for the sides and angles of the original triangle; for example, we obtain thus the formula
{{block center|<math>\cos 4A = \frac{a^2\cos^2 A\cos^2 2A-b^2\cos^2 B\cos^2 2B-c^2\cos^2 C\cos^2 2C}{2bc\cos B\cos C\cos 2B\cos 2C}</math>.}}
This transformation obviously admits of further extension.

'''''Solution of Triangles.'''''

(1) The three sides of a triangle <math>ABC</math> being given, the angles can be determined by the formula {{block center|<math>L \tan \frac{1}{2}A = 10 + \frac{1}{2} \log (s-b) + \frac{1}{2} \log (s-c) - \frac{1}{2} \log s - \frac{1}{2} \log (s-a)</math>}}
and two corresponding formulae for the other angles.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
